solution: The **stigma** (the stigmatic surface of the pistil). It recognises and accepts compatible pollen of the same species and refuses wrong or incompatible pollen, the compatibility being determined by special proteins.

**Six** haploid cells: the egg cell, two synergids and three antipodal cells. The seventh cell, the large central cell, contains the diploid **secondary nucleus** formed by the fusion of the two polar nuclei.

Each ovule needs **both** male gametes of one pollen tube: one fuses with the egg (**syngamy**) and the other fuses with the secondary nucleus (**triple fusion**). Since one pollen grain forms one pollen tube that enters one ovule, both its male gametes are used up in that single ovule, so 20 ovules need at least 20 pollen grains.

**Megasporogenesis** is the process of formation of haploid megaspores from the diploid **megaspore mother cell (MMC)** by meiosis. The MMC lies in the nucellus of the ovule and forms a linear tetrad of megaspores, of which one remains functional.

**Hydrophily** is pollination by water. It is found only in some 30 genera of aquatic monocots, e.g. *Vallisneria*, *Zostera*, *Ceratophyllum*, and is of two types, **hypohydrophily** (below the water surface) and **epihydrophily** (on the water surface).
The **tapetum**. It is the innermost nutritive layer of the anther wall and immediately encloses the sporogenous tissue (microspore mother cells).

**Parthenocarpy** is the condition in which a fruit develops without the process of fertilization. Such a fruit resembles a normal fruit but is **seedless**, e.g. some varieties of pineapple, banana and papaya. The term was coined by Noll (1902).

No. **Apomixis** is the formation of embryo(s) by an asexual method, without formation of gametes and without the act of fertilization (no meiosis and syngamy), so fertilization is not needed, and pollination, whose role is to bring gametes together for fertilization, is not needed either.
[Note: the chapter does not state in so many words whether pollination is required in apomixis; the answer follows from its definition of apomixis as reproduction without gametes and fertilization.]

The **ovary** develops into the **fruit** (its wall becoming the pericarp) and the **ovules** develop into the **seeds**. After fertilization the ovule is transformed into the seed and the ovary into the fruit.
The **filiform apparatus** is the group of hair like projections of the synergids. It **guides the pollen tube towards the egg**.

**Polyembryony** is the occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed, which results in the emergence of multiple seedlings. In **adventive polyembryony**, as in *Citrus*, embryos develop directly from diploid cells of the nucellus and integuments, so they carry only the parent's genes. Therefore **genetically uniform, parental type seedlings** are obtained from these nucellar embryos, and genetically identical plants can be produced effectively and rapidly. For this reason **nucellar adventive polyembryony is of great significance in horticulture**, e.g. in Mango, Orange and Lemon. Polyembryony also increases the chances of survival of the new plants.

Flowers must be pollinated in order to produce seeds and fruit. **Pollination** is the prerequisite for fertilization, because both the male and female gametes are non-motile and are produced at two different sites. **Seed development is initiated by fertilization**: the fertilized ovule becomes the seed and its integuments form the seed coat. **Fruit development is triggered by hormones produced by the developing seeds**, under which the ovary differentiates into the fruit and the ovary wall into the pericarp. Thus, without pollination there is no fertilization, without fertilization no seeds, and without developing seeds no normal fruit. (Parthenocarpy is the exception: such fruits form without fertilization, but they are seedless.)

Pollination does not guarantee transfer of the right type of pollen; wrong types also land on the stigma. The pistil can **recognise and accept the compatible pollen of the same species** and discard the wrong or incompatible pollen, the compatibility and incompatibility being determined by **special proteins**. A physiological mechanism ensures that only intraspecific pollen germinates successfully, so an incompatible pollen grain does not germinate or its tube does not grow, and its male gametes never reach the egg. In **self incompatibility (self sterility)**, a genetic mechanism inhibits the germination of pollen on the stigma of the same flower, e.g. Tobacco, *Thea*. Thus incompatibility acts as a **natural barrier** that prevents fusion of unsuitable gametes.

1. **Unisexuality (dioecism)**: the flowers are unisexual, bearing either stamens or carpels, so self pollination is not possible. Plants may be monoecious, e.g. Maize, or dioecious, e.g. Mulberry, Papaya.
2. **Dichogamy**: in a bisexual flower the anthers and stigma mature at different times. In **protandry** the androecium matures first, e.g. disc florets of sunflower; in **protogyny** the gynoecium matures first, e.g. *Gloriosa*.
3. **Herkogamy**: a natural physical barrier between the two sex organs of a bisexual flower prevents contact of its pollen with its own stigma, e.g. in *Calotropis* the pentangular stigma is positioned above the level of the anthers (pollinia).

Other such devices are prepotency, heterostyly and self incompatibility.

**Double fertilization** is the fertilization mechanism of flowering (angiospermic) plants in which **both male gametes** take part. It was discovered by Nawaschin in liliaceous plants like *Lilium* and *Fritillaria*.

1. A compatible pollen grain on the stigma germinates and forms a **pollen tube**, which penetrates the stigma, style and ovary chamber and enters the ovule.
2. Its growth is guided by chemicals secreted by the synergids. It usually enters the ovule through the micropyle (**porogamy**), in some cases through the chalaza (**chalazogamy**) or by piercing the integuments (**mesogamy**).
3. The tube penetrates the embryo sac at its micropylar end and enters one of the **synergids**, absorbs its watery contents, then ruptures and releases its contents, including the **two non-motile male gametes**. Carrying non-motile gametes through the hollow tube is called **siphonogamy**.
4. **Syngamy**: one haploid male gamete fuses with the haploid egg to form the **diploid zygote**, which develops into the embryo (generative fertilization).
5. **Triple fusion**: the second haploid male gamete fuses with the **diploid secondary nucleus** to form the **triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)**, which develops into the endosperm (vegetative fertilization).

Since syngamy and triple fusion both occur in the same embryo sac, the process is called double fertilization. It is a unique feature of angiosperms: it restores the diploid condition in the zygote and ensures that the seed is given a food store (endosperm) only if the egg is fertilized.

The **microspore (pollen grain)** is a non-motile, haploid, unicellular body with a single nucleus, surrounded by the two layered **sporoderm**: a thick outer **exine** of sporopollenin with thin **germ pores**, and an inner **intine** of cellulose and pectin. The pollen grain marks the beginning of the **male gametophyte**.

1. **First mitotic division**: the pollen grain nucleus divides to produce a bigger **vegetative cell** and a small, thin walled **generative cell**. The vegetative cell is rich in food and has an irregular shaped nucleus; the generative cell floats in the cytoplasm of the vegetative cell.
2. **Shedding**: in most angiosperms the pollen grains are shed from the anther at this **two-celled stage**.
3. **Germination**: on the stigma the pollen grain forms a **pollen tube** that grows out through a germ pore; the vegetative nucleus lies in the tube as the **tube nucleus**.
4. **Second mitotic division**: this concerns the generative cell only and gives rise to **two non-motile male gametes**. It takes place either in the pollen grain or in the pollen tube.

The germinated pollen grain with its tube nucleus and two male gametes is the mature male gametophyte.

The development of the zygote into an embryo is called **embryogenesis**. In a dicot, as in *Capsella*, it takes place at the micropylar end of the embryo sac after some endosperm has formed.

1. The zygote (oospore) divides to form a **two-celled proembryo**: a larger **basal or suspensor initial** towards the micropyle and a smaller **terminal or embryonal initial** towards the chalaza.
2. The suspensor initial divides transversely to form a filamentous **suspensor** of 6-10 cells. Its first cell, towards the micropyle, swells and acts as a **haustorium**; its lowermost cell is the **hypophysis**. The suspensor pushes the embryo into the endosperm.
3. The embryonal initial undergoes three successive mitotic divisions, in planes at right angles to each other, to form an **octant** of eight cells.
4. The lower tier of four cells gives rise to the **hypocotyl and radicle**, and the upper tier of four cells forms the **plumule and cotyledons**.
5. The hypophysis divides further to give rise to part of the **radicle and the root cap**.
6. The cells of the upper tier divide in several planes so that the embryo becomes **heart shaped**, forming two lateral cotyledons and a terminal plumule.
7. Further enlargement of the hypocotyl and cotyledons curves the embryo, which becomes **horse-shoe shaped**.

Finally the ovule is transformed into the seed and the ovary into the fruit.

**Diagram**: the L.S. of an anatropous ovule (book Fig. 1.6), with the micropyle directed downwards next to the funicle. Labels: **chalaza, nucellus, outer integument, inner integument, embryo sac, antipodals, secondary nucleus, synergids, egg, micropyle, hilum, funicle, placenta**.

**Components of the embryo sac and their fate after fertilization:**

| Component | Fate after fertilization |
|---|---|
| **Egg** (one, haploid, at the micropylar end) | fuses with one male gamete (syngamy) to form the diploid **zygote**, which develops into the **embryo** |
| **Two synergids** (haploid, with filiform apparatus) | one receives the pollen tube; they disorganize |
| **Central cell with the secondary nucleus** (diploid, formed by fusion of the two polar nuclei) | the secondary nucleus fuses with the second male gamete (triple fusion) to form the triploid **primary endosperm nucleus**, which develops into the **endosperm** |
| **Three antipodal cells** (haploid, at the chalazal end) | disorganize |

The egg and the two synergids together form the **egg apparatus**. After fertilization the other cells of the embryo sac disorganize sooner or later, the integuments of the ovule become the seed coat and the ovule becomes the seed.

The figure shows a bean seed (dicot, non-endospermic): an entire seed in external view (left) and the same seed opened to show the embryo (right).

| Pointer | Label |

| Folded leaf like structure at the top of the opened seed | **Plumule** |
| Curved, pointed tip of the embryonic axis (top right) | **Radicle** |
| Small structure in the seed coat beside the radicle tip | **Micropyle** |

| Thin inner covering next to the cotyledon (bottom) | **Tegmen** (inner seed coat) |

The plumule, radicle and cotyledons together form the **embryo**; the testa and tegmen form the **seed coat**, and the micropyle persists as a small pore in it that lets in water and oxygen during soaking. Reading notes: the top right pointer lands on the bend just above the tip, so it may also be read as the **hypocotyl** (the axis between plumule and radicle); the two lower pointers both reach the seed covering, and they are read as testa (outer) and tegmen (inner), either of which may be labelled simply **seed coat**.
